title: Linguistic Internalism and Externalism: Bridging Medieval and Contemporary Thought
location: Jackman Humanities Building 100
description:
Join us for a one-day workshop on linguistic internalism and externalism featuring Peter King (University of Toronto), Gyula Klima (Fordham University), Simone L. Migliaro (Humboldt University, Berlin – University of Toronto), Calvin Normore (University of California, Los Angeles), Claude Panaccio (Université du Québec à Montreal), and Giorgio Pini (Fordham University). 
The distinction between internalism and externalism has shaped much of the contemporary analytic debate on the nature and function of language. Internalism encompasses theories holding that the meaning of an expression is primarily determined by internal states—more simply, by what is in the speaker’s mind. Externalism, by contrast, assigns greater weight to factors outside the subject, such as the linguistic community or causal relations to the external world. This distinction initially emerged to contrast the descriptivist and broadly internalist approaches of authors such as Gottlob Frege or Noam Chomsky with the externalist accounts developed by Saul Kripke and Hilary Putnam. 
The debate, however, remains vibrant and continues to inspire new interpretations and refinements. There is broad agreement that, by the late Middle Ages, a coherent and systematic approach to the analysis of language and its proprerties had begun to develop. This development produced a sophisticated theoretical framework, traditionally known as logica modernorum, and sparked new debates that challenged several assumptions of the Aristotelian tradition. Prevailing positions held that linguistic meaning was essentially determined by concepts—and thus by the subject’s internal cognitive grasp—yet this account did not seem to convince authors such as John Duns Scotus or William of Ockham. Some scholars have therefore proposed classifying their theories as externalist, in order to distinguish them from more traditional internalist accounts. This interpretative move, however, has not been universally accepted and has at times faced substantial methodological criticism. 
This workshop aims to advance the discussion by creating a forum for exchange between experts in contemporary analytic philosophy and scholars of medieval thought. Framed around the internalism-externalism distinction, it seeks to evaluate how effectively this framework can illuminate medieval theories of language. While the structural parallels between certain contemporary analyses and late medieval developments are undeniable, it remains to be determined how philosophically fruitful and historically justified these comparisons are, and whether the conceptual differences between the two contexts constitute a limitation or, conversely, a theoretical opportunity. 
Questions the workshop aims to answer: • What do we mean by internalism and externalism? • To what extent can medieval theories of language be meaningfully classified in terms of the internalism–externalism dichotomy? • To what extent do medieval theories resemble contemporary accounts? And in what respects do they differ? • Are these differences a limitation or an opportunity?

title: Digital Expo: AI & Democracy
location: Toronto Reference Library, Appel Salon, Second Floor
description:
Join leading experts for thought-provoking panel discussions exploring the impact of AI on safety, democracy, civic participation, trust and human flourishing. This registration provides access to all four panel discussions and the exhibitor showcase.
Can't attend in person? The panels will also be livestreamed.
Register to receive the viewing link
.
Panel discussions
Helping Children Navigate AI Safely
11:15 am-12 pm
Explore how AI is shaping children's lives and learn practical ways to support safe, responsible and informed AI use at home and in school.
Featuring Matthew Johnson (MediaSmarts), André Côté (The Dais), and Aarani Stoneham (AI Literacy Learners), with moderation by Jessica Wong (CBC).
Safeguarding Democracy in the Age of AI
1-1:45 pm
Join this keynote to examine the opportunities and risks AI presents for democracy, and the steps needed to strengthen trust, safety and civic participation.
Featuring Beatrice Wayne (Samara Centre for Democracy) and Valentine Goddard (AI Impact Alliance).
AI and Civic Engagement
2-3 pm
Learn how AI is changing the way people access information, engage with one another and participate in democracy.
Featuring Mathew Markman (Ethelo), Trevor Potts (Evidence for Democracy) and Lexa Michaelides (Hypha), with moderation by Tai Huynh (The Local).
Flourishing in an AI Society
3:15-4:15 pm
Discover how communities can help guide AI development toward human flourishing, trust and democratic values.
Featuring Victória Oldemburgo de Mello (Work and Play Lab), Jess Mitchell (OCAD University), Stephanie Jonnson (ODLAN) and Mario Vasilescu (Readocracy), with moderation by Pete Bombaci (Genwell).

9:30 am-4:30 pm

title: Digital Expo: AI & Democracy (Livestream)
description:
Join our Digital Expo panel discussions via livestream from anywhere. Discover how AI is shaping safety, democracy, civic participation and trust, and explore how we can build AI that advances human flourishing.
Registrants will receive an email with a Zoom meeting link within 24 hours before the program starts.
Looking to attend in person?
Learn more and register
.
Panel discussions:
Helping Children Navigate AI Safely
11:15 am-12 pm
Explore how AI is shaping children's lives and learn practical ways to support safe, responsible and informed AI use at home and in school.
Featuring Matthew Johnson (MediaSmarts), André Côté (The Dais), and Aarani Stoneham (AI Literacy Learners), with moderation by Jessica Wong (CBC).
Safeguarding Democracy in the Age of AI
1-1:45 pm
Join this keynote to examine the opportunities and risks AI presents for democracy, and the steps needed to strengthen trust, safety and civic participation.
Featuring Beatrice Wayne (Samara Centre for Democracy) and Valentine Goddard (AI Impact Alliance).
AI and Civic Engagement
2-3 pm
Learn how AI is changing the way people access information, engage with one another and participate in democracy.
Featuring Mathew Markman (Ethelo), Trevor Potts (Evidence for Democracy) and Lexa Michaelides (Hypha), with moderation by Tai Huynh (The Local).
Flourishing in an AI Society
3:15-4:15 pm
Discover how communities can help guide AI development toward human flourishing, trust and democratic values.
Featuring Victória Oldemburgo de Mello (Work and Play Lab), Jess Mitchell (OCAD University), Stephanie Jonnson (ODLAN) and Mario Vasilescu (Readocracy), with moderation by Pete Bombaci (Genwell).

title: Livestream Viewing: Japanese Canadian Monument Opening Ceremony
location: Japanese Canadian Cultural Centre
description:
Announcement for unveiling of the Japanese Canadian Monument *Momiji Capacity has been reached, it is now waitlist only! Please join us at the Japanese Canadian Cultural Centre (JCCC) or Momiji Health Care Society (Momiji) on Saturday, October 3, 2026 at 3:30pm EST for the live streaming of the opening ceremony of the Japanese Canadian Monument that is taking place in Victoria, British Columbia. A pre-show program will begin at 3:30pm, and the opening ceremony livestream will begin at 4:00pm. Further information per livestream location is outlined below. The Japanese Canadian Monument lists the names of all Japanese Canadians uprooted in 1942 AND a second set of names of children born after uprooting and up to and including March 31, 1949, after which freedom to return to the coast was fully granted. The monument acknowledges the forced dispossession and internment of the community during World War II while celebrating their resilience and impact on the region. These names and locations engraved on the wall provide a stark illustration of a community torn apart by policies that were driven by a confluence of race, economics, and power. To set them in stone here is to ensure they are never again forgotten or marginalized. Please register from the button below to attend the Japanese Canadian Monument opening ceremony livestream: Register Light refreshments will be served, and a souvenir book will be gifted to all attendees. Please note that capacity will be limited based on location selected ( choice between JCCC and Momiji (Waitlist Only) ) . Registration will open at 2:00pm EST on August 24, 2026 and will close at 11:00am EST on September 24, 2026 or once capacity at each location is reached, whichever comes first. For more information, please refer to https://hcmc.uvic.ca/project/monument/ . For any questions, please reach out to jccc@jccc.on.ca . Livestream Event Information at the JCCC: Thank you for joining the JCCC at the monument unveiling livestream on Saturday, October 3, 2026! Doors will open at 2:30pm EST on October 3, 2026 for sign in, and the pre-show program and livestream will begin at 3:30pm EST in Kobayashi Hall. Light refreshments will be served, and a souvenir book will be gifted to all attendees. Please note that the maximum capacity of the livestream event in Kobayashi Hall is 300 guests. Once the registration form reaches maximum capacity, a waitlist for 50 guests will be monitored. Registrants will be contacted via email in September to confirm their entrance status (enrolled or waitlist) . Further details will be communicated via email, e-blast, and social media in September. The JCCC will also be replaying the livestream throughout the evening beginning at 7:00pm EST on October 3, 2026 during Nuit Blanche, as well as during Issei Day on October 4, 2026. Registration is not required for Nuit Blanche livestream viewing on October 3, 2026. To register for Issei Day, please visit: Issei Day page . A souvenir book will also be gifted to all Issei Day attendees on October 4, 2026. We look forward to seeing you there! Livestream Event Information at Momiji Health Care Society: *Momiji Capacity has been reached, now waitlist only! Momiji would like to welcome our community to watch the livestream of the monument unveiling in Victoria, BC, from the comfort of the Yone and Coby Kobayashi Auditorium at Momiji Seniors Residence. Momiji will be providing a small, boxed meal for the first 150 community members and 70 tenants registered. Once we hit capacity, a waitlist will be created, and we will be working with the JCCC to ensure that as many people as possible are able to watch the event. Since the event is overlapping with our annual bazaar, we are inviting attendees to arrive anytime from Noon to 3:00pm and support our annual bazaar before joining the livestream. Further details will be communicated by email and social media in September.

Language Exchangeへようこそ！このグループでは、皆さんのレベルに応じて、3〜4名のグループにわかれ、同じ席になった人たちで各45分間、それぞれ英語と日本語でフリートークを行なっていただきます。決まったディスカッショントピックなどはございませんので、気軽に質問をしながらそれぞれのセッションを楽しんでいただければと思います。

予約規約（⚠️重要）

・当日の不参加、もしくは15分以上の遅刻、また予約取消締切後の変更は原則不参加(No-Show)とみなします。不参加(No-show)が3回になりますと会員登録が抹消され、退会となりますのでご注意ください。

・空席ができた際は、自動的に”キャンセル待ち”より”参加予定”へ変更されます。この時にMeetupよりお知らせがあるかはわかりません。

・システムにより自動的に”参加予定”とされ、それに気づかずに参加しなかった場合でも、不参加とみなされますのでご了承ください。

ぜひこちらもフォローお願いします！

***Although our group is a non-profit organization, we collect $ 5 per English Speaker for every event. All the proceeds are used to run this website and for social events***

This is an in-person language exchange! Members are placed into groups of three or four based on their language level. Each 45 minute session consists of friendly casual conversation, and/or informal study.

title: Paradise
location: Japanese Canadian Cultural Centre
description:
The JCCC Gallery's fall exhibition is Paradise : a multimedia installation by Japanese Canadian artists and longtime family friends Mitchell Akiyama and Emma Nishimura that explores intergenerational inheritance. Combining print, video, and sculpture, the work reflects on their relationship to the legacy of Japanese Canadian internment experienced by their paternal grandparents. The exhibition draws on a shared childhood memory of a summer day in Northern Ontario, where the artists and their siblings built a temporary “Frog Paradise.” This moment of play, shaped by a sense of safety and belonging, becomes a lens for considering how one group’s utopia can exist alongside another’s harm. The installation includes video that intercuts footage of this experience with recent visits to former internment sites in British Columbia. Bridging personal narrative and historical context, Paradise examines the forced relocation and incarceration of Japanese Canadians, tracing how this legacy continues to shape memory, displacement, and belonging across generations. Please join us for our opening reception on October 25 th from 2 to 4 pm Opening Reception More programming to be announced shortly!

TORONTO ARTS & CULTURE
We will start off the 26/27 Koerner Hall concert season, with a performance by Vieux Farka Touré (from Mali), and opening for him is Melat Mengesha (from Ethiopia)

(And we have our eyes on other concerts during the season!)

Also we have a 15% off ticket promo!! ***Ticket link is below*--($50-$80)**

Known worldwide for his electrifying live shows, Vieux Farka Touré’s virtuosic guitar work blends Malian blues, rock, and soul. Winner of Ethiopian Idol Melat Mengesha opens the show.

Often referred to as “The Hendrix of the Sahara,” **Vieux Farka Touré** is the son of legendary Malian guitarist Ali Farka Touré, who died in 2006. His live performances are highly energized, and Vieux is known for dazzling crowds with his speed and dexterity on the guitar, as well as his palpable charisma and luminous smile, both of which captivate audiences despite any language barriers (though Vieux does speak eight languages!).

Hailing from Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, now based in Toronto, \*\*Melat Mengesha’\*\*s music features contemporary, folk, and Ethio-jazz roots sounds. Two major influences in her artistic expression are the legendary Ethiopian singers Gigi (Ejigayehu Shibabaw) and Aster Aweke. A major turning point came in 2015, when Melat won the first season of Balageru (Ethiopian Idol). That breakthrough opened the door to a variety of showcases and performances, from intimate stages to large-scale concerts, allowing her to tour across her hometown and beyond.

title: Bus Hike: Limehouse (Bruce Trail Day)
description:
Toronto Bruce Trail Club
oin us to celebrate Bruce Trail Day on the trail around Limehouse. For the first 5 km we will hike south from the Sixth Line to Limehouse. The route incorporates the portion of trail removed from the Fifth Line thanks to those who support the Bruce Trail. We'll also pass the seed orchard where native species are grown for the seeds to be replanted to re-naturalize other parts of the trail. Those who want a shorter hike may drop out at Limehouse where information and refreshments will be available at the Memorial Hall. The second part of the hike will be a loop through the Limehouse Conservation area featuring the limestone kilns, stone arched bridge, and a climb through the "hole in the wall". Expect some slightly rocky terrain underfoot and a few moderate hills. Hiking boots or good shoes designed for walking are a must. Those completing the full 9 km will also have a chance to drop in at the Memorial Hall to learn more about the Bruce Trail and refreshments.

You must register and prepay the bus fare on the Bruce Trail Conservancy Website (registration opens Sat Sep 20 8:00 PM (Bus Fares $25 Members/$32 Non-Members (Children under 12 $10/$14). Bus fares are non-refundable and the hike goes rain or shine.

title: Devils Hole - US Side
description:
These Boots Are Made for Hiking
Meetup: **Niagara Gorge - US side**
Meet up point: Devil's Hole State Park Parking Area
Address: 5100 Niagara Scenic Pkwy, Niagara Falls, NY 14305, United States
GPS Coordinates: 43.13301222763603, -79.04771831578047 (or 43°07'58.8"N 79°02'51.8"W)
**Make sure you have your passport!**
We usually hike the Canadian side, so we decided we needed a different point of view!
Devil’s Hole is a semi-circular notch formed by an ancient waterfall draining a section of Glacial Lake Tonawanda. This waterfall formed as the main Falls eroded back past this point in the gorge. Lake Tonawanda eventually dried up along with its waterfall.
In the early 1700's, the raging waters so terrified the locals that it was supposed that the devil lived there. The name stuck.
**Legend and Lore of Devil’s Hole**
**Devil’s Hole Massacre:** On September 14, 1763, a British supply train of wagons was passing by Devil’s Hole when a band of Senecas ambushed the party, killing all but a few who escaped (2 or 3). The commotion was heard by soldiers stationed near the head of the Portage in Lewiston and reinforcements were sent marching up the road in formation. These troops were also attacked and basically wiped out.

title: Traditional Indigo Batik Workshop
location: Toronto Botanical Garden, 777 Lawrence Avenue East, Toronto, ON, M3C 1P2, Canada
description:
Join us for an fun-filled workshop and introduction to the traditional practice of indigo batik!
Indigo batik is a captivating textile art form that combines the beauty of natural indigo dyeing with intricate wax-resist designs. Its origins can be traced back to ancient civilizations across various cultures and regions, including Egypt, China, India, and West Africa around 2,000 years ago.
 
The technique gained prominence in Southeast Asia, particularly in Java, Indonesia, where the intricate art form of “batik tulis” (hand-drawn batik) evolved and is now a widely recognized intangible cultural heritage.
 
Batik is also widely practiced by the Miao indigenous group in Southwest China and holds historical and cultural significance for these communities to this day. Girls would learn the art of batik from their moms starting at the age of eight or nine. Since the Miao does not have their own written language, the Miao women have had a large role to play in documenting their people’s history, stories, and emotions through their textile arts.
 
During this 3-hour workshop, you will learn about the history and traditional motifs of Miao batik, as well as a significant hands-on portion dedicated to learning the traditional wax-resist dyeing method. You will create patterns using batik tools from the Miao community, before dyeing your finished piece in natural indigo.
 
No prior knowledge is needed to take this workshop, and all materials will be provided.
 
Attendees are encouraged to think through some patterns and designs they would like to work on during the session but we will also provide additional ideas and motifs for inspiration.
 
We will provide all materials, such as natural beeswax, small electric pots, batik painting tools (“ladao”), indigo dye bath, and an iron. Additionally, each participant is provided with upcycled, practice fabrics as well as a piece of organic cotton handkerchief to create on.
 
Sunday, October 4, 1 to 4:30 p.m.
Public $120, TBG Members $115 (plus applicable taxes and fees).
 
About Lisa Shi
Lisa Shi is the co-founder of SlowMaking, a cultural platform dedicated to preserving and sharing traditional craft knowledge. She has spent years travelling, learning, and conducting field research on cultural craft traditions, exploring how material culture and techniques reveal universal threads of connection across global communities.
 
Her engagement with batik is grounded in firsthand study with both Chinese and Indonesian researchers and artisans. These cross-cultural experiences inform her global understanding of batik and its broader textile histories, influences, and techniques, shaping a teaching practice rooted in research, respect, and hands-on experimentation.
 
About SlowMaking
At SlowMaking, we inspire intercultural connections and a slow, sustainable way of life through authentic storytelling, artisanal products, and immersive experiences that centre around heritage crafts.
 
To follow along for more cultural crafts and traditions: Instagram | Youtube | Website

A TBG membership helps you deepen your knowledge and connection to the natural world, become a part of a dynamic community of plant people, and be inspired! Become a member!

title: Bring Your Problem: Can AI Help?
location: North York Central Library, 2nd Floor eLearning Lab
description:
Do you have a recurring problem you think AI might help with? A thing you keep doing by hand that feels like it should be easier? Bring it. If you don't have one, come help your neighbours with theirs.
In this interactive class, you'll learn a simple seven-step way to think about problems: what's annoying you, what you've tried, what AI could actually do, and where it would fail. We'll gather real problems from the room, sort them into groups, and map out what's worth solving with AI, and what's better solved without it. We'll also talk honestly about what an AI fix costs: your money, your time, and sometimes your private information. The problems AI could help with most are often the most personal, and the most personal ones are worth the most care.
Registration is required and will start September 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM.
Note: Your spot will not be guaranteed after 5 minutes of the start of the program.

title: Doug Johnstone (DNRC Herzberg)
location: MP1318A
description:
Title: The Variability of Deeply Embedded Protostars: Past, Present, and Future

Abstract: Using the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope (JCMT) we have monitored eight nearby low-mass star-forming regions in the Gould
Belt at submillimetre wavelengths for almost a decade to search for and quantify the time dependent brightness
variability of the resident deeply embedded protostars. Secular variability is common among these protostars; greater
than 25% of the sample show measurable long-term brightness changes and 10% show burst behaviour lasting from months 
to years. We interpret this secular variability as reflecting changes in the mass accretion rate from the disk to the
protostar, as predicted by theoretical models of (proto)stellar assembly. For a subset of our sample we have
contemporaneous mid-IR light-curves which allow additional constraints on the conditions responsible for the brightness
variations, confirming that the submillimetre variability is driven by changes in the dust temperature profile of the
envelope. Furthermore, we have combined, for one source, single dish and interferometric sub-mm monitoring, which
has allowed us to unambiguously recover a time lag in the variability at larger angular scales and use the results to
confirm the envelope structure surrounding the embedded protostar.
Host: Shantanu Basu

title: Postcards of Reconnection: A Craft Workshop
location: North York Central Library, Concourse Event Space, North York Central Library (5120 Yonge St).
description:
Postcards of Reconnection
Sometimes reconnecting starts in solitude, not small talk. In this quiet, reflective craft workshop, you’ll design and illustrate a postcard for someone you've been meaning to reach: a friend, a family member, or anyone lingering in your thoughts. Take it home, add a stamp when you're ready and pop it into the mail, taking the first step towards an important reconnection.
This interactive pre-show is followed by
From Solitude To Connetion ft. Robert Coplan,
which starts at 7pm in the North York Central Library Concourse.
You can register for that event
here
, but please note if you wish to attend the postcard workshop you need to register separately
on this page
.
***
Spend an evening rethinking time alone in a room full of other people
, as
we exp
lore the
theme
of
“good solitude” and how alone time makes togetherness possible
.
Make the most of your
Connect IRL
experience by coming before or staying after the
featured event
. Grab a drink or snack at the bar. Sign up for the workshop or try out one of the engagement activities available, including the Conversation Station: The Calming Corner, where you can take a moment or two to connect with a stranger around the topic of solitude.
The
C
alming
Corner
| 5:30 – 6:30 pm & 8:00 – 9:00 pm
The Calming Corner offers a calmer, low-sensory space with small seating pods of two or three, prompt cards on solitude and recharge habits, and no pressure to mingle beyond your comfort zone. It's built on Coplan's own research that meaningful connection doesn't require constant stimulation, just the right amount of space to think before you speak.
Connect IRL
is not your average series of events, workshops and activities, but a real chance to connect with other Torontonians in meaningful and sometimes unexpected ways. Through conversation stations meant to spark one-on-one conversations, or hands-on engagement activities and workshops before the featured event, participants can explore the value of connection and community.

description:
Clayming Love

6:00 pm – 8:00 pm
 

                
                    
    



    
         
    




    
        
             
                
                    For ages 18+ 
Are you ready? Are you open? Are you willing? 
“The awareness in our hands is alive and continuous. The feeling of our lives will be awake in our fingers. We befriend the clay. The clay befriends us.” — M.C. Richards 
The sense of touch cannot happen anywhere but the here and now. Touch is immediate. Through exploration with clay we will recognize how we can be stuck because we have not looked deeply enough into the nature of our experience. 
Guided by a Zen Buddhist practitioner and registered art therapist, engage in clay exercises designed to call attention to habits of belief, judgments, and the stories we tell ourselves. With self-compassion, we will create possibilities to loosen their hold on us by working with the malleability of clay. 
At the end of the workshop we return the clay to its original form, letting go of what was created and ready to begin anew. 
This workshop welcomes everyone, whether you are new to or familiar with clay, breath, and presence.

                    Suzanne Thomson is ceramic artist, registered psychotherapist, and art therapist with over 30 years of experience integrating these practices to facilitate healing, community building and social transformation work. As a practitioner of Zen Buddhism with training in contemplative arts, sensorimotor psychotherapy, narrative therapy, and trauma-informed approaches she offers psychotherapy, clinical supervision, and has taught at the Toronto Art Therapy Institute and the University of Toronto. title: From Solitude To Connetion ft. Robert Coplan
location: North York Central Library, Concourse Event Space, North York Central Library (5120 Yonge St), Lower Level
description:
Spend an evening rethinking time alone in a room full of other people as we explore the theme of “good solitude” and how alone time makes togetherness possible.
Make the most of your
Connect IRL
experience by coming before or staying after the featured event. Grab a drink or snack at the bar.
Sign up for the Postcards of Re-Connections Workshop
(see below for registration) or try out one of the engagement activities available, including the
Conversation
Station:
The
C
alming
Corner
, where you can take a moment or two to connect with a stranger around the topic of solitude.
****
Join us at the North York Central Library Concourse for
Being Alone Together
with psychologist and author Robert Coplan
in conversation with Alanna Mitchell
.
Together, we’ll take apart the assumption that solitude and connection pull in opposite directions, examine the difference between chosen alone time and painful disconnection, and talk about how much of each we actually need. Expect to leave with a clearer sense of your own limits, and a few practical ways to protect the quiet that makes company possible.
What does "good" solitude actually look like, and how is it different from the isolation so many people are struggling with? How do extraverts and introverts experience alone time differently, and what do we get wrong about both? And in a culture that treats constant availability as a virtue, what would it mean to reclaim solitude as a skill worth practicing — not an escape from community, but a foundation for building it?
Coplan, a Carleton University psychologist and one of the world's leading researchers on solitude, draws on psychology, neuroscience, literature and sociology in The Joy of Solitude: How to Reconnect with Yourself in an Overconnected World. He distinguishes loneliness from solitude, introduces "aloneliness" — the real distress of not having enough time to yourself — and shows that even fifteen minutes alone a day can stabilize mood, spark creativity and recharge our capacity for connection.
Come for a thoughtful conversation about the surprising role alone time plays in helping us feel closer to others.
Q&A to follow. Books available for purchase.

The Calming Corner offers a calmer, low-sensory space with small seating pods of two or three, prompt cards on solitude and recharge habits, and no pressure to mingle beyond your comfort zone. It's built on Coplan's own research that meaningful connection doesn't require constant stimulation, just the right amount of space to think before you speak.
Connect IRL
is not your average series of events, workshops and activities, but a real chance to connect with other Torontonians in meaningful and sometimes unexpected ways. Through conversation stations meant to spark one-on-one conversations, or hands-on engagement activities and workshops before the featured event, participants can explore the value of connection and community.

title: Does Canada Need a National Portrait Gallery?
location: Toronto Reference Library, Appel Salon, Second Floor
description:
Join four leading voices to imagine what could be one of Canada’s most significant cultural institutions yet to be built.
Canadians are experiencing a renewed sense of who we are and why it matters to be us – is now the time to respond to decades of demand for a National Portrait Gallery?
While the majority of countries include portraits of their 'great and good' in their history museums, art galleries, archives and monuments; some countries have chosen a more democratic path – creating stand-alone National Institutions in their capital cities that celebrate not only the political and military greats, but also the change-makers in every walk of life, age, ethnicity and talent. Canada has no institutional equivalent – is this a quiet statement about our national character and preference for practical leadership over hero-worship, or a decentralized sense of identity that resists a single national narrative? Or is it simply an overlooked institutional gap that deserves to be filled?
Acclaimed UK-based architect Jamie Fobert, celebrated Indigenous curator and historian Tim Johnson, and writer and activist Sarah Lazarovic join moderator Gail Lord for a wide-ranging conversation about what such an institution could mean for the country.
Together they’ll examine the case for a National Portrait Gallery: what it might contain, how it could meaningfully include and center Indigenous voices and communities, where it might be located, and how it could be funded and supported – including whether the political will currently exists to make it a reality. The panel will also consider what a distinctly Canadian portrait gallery might look like in contrast to its counterparts in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, and what unique story it could tell about the nation and its people.
Q&A to follow.

Sarah Lazarovic

Oct 7 - AI for the Non-Technical

"Elephant in the Room"

"AI for Good"
mindset. We demystify the technology by viewing AI as an

title: Oct 8 - MCP, Agents and Skills Meetup Meetup
description:
Toronto AI, Machine Learning and Computer Vision Meetup
Join our virtual meetup to hear talks from experts on MCP, agents and skills.

**Date, Time and Location**

Oct 08, 2026
9:00 AM - 11:00 AM PST
Online. **[Register for the Zoom!](https://voxel51.com/events/mcp-agents-skills-meetup-october-8-2026)**

**Designing Multi‑Agent Systems: Sequential, Parallel, and Beyond with ADK**

Multi‑agent systems are powerful but choosing the wrong interaction pattern can quickly lead to fragile, slow, or expensive AI systems.
In this talk, we explore the core multi‑agent design patterns enabled by ADK, including sequential, parallel, and more advanced coordination models. Rather than focusing on tools alone, we’ll look at how to think architecturally about agent collaboration.

You’ll learn:

* When sequential agents are the right choice and when they become a bottleneck
* How parallel agents improve speed and coverage (and the trade‑offs they introduce)
* Common failure modes in poorly designed agent interactions
* Practical criteria for choosing the right pattern based on task, latency, and reliability

By the end of the session, you’ll have a clear mental model for designing multi‑agent systems that are intentional, scalable, and production‑ready.

*About the Speaker*

[Dr Roushanak Rahmat](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roushanakrahmat/) is an Enterprise AI Architect, Google Developer Expert (AI & Cloud), and recognized among the Top 100 Women in Tech (2025). With a PhD in Artificial Intelligence and over 15 years of experience, she specializes in designing and delivering enterprise-scale Generative AI, Agentic AI, and Deep Learning solutions that transform industries including healthcare, finance, energy, and public services.

**Privacy by Deployment: Architecting Agent-Driven Localization Workflows for Regulated Environments**

Most enterprise AI today is private by promise - a DPA, a SOC 2 report, or a contract clause that says, "we won't train on your data". For a regulated buyer, these are remedies after a breach, not controls that prevent or contain one. For organizations in healthcare, finance, defense, and government, privacy often requires stronger guarantees: data residency, customer-controlled execution, and, in some cases, operation within air-gapped environments.

This session demonstrates how agentic AI can automate a localization workflow while operating within these constraints. Using a real-world localization pipeline as an example, we will show how agentic systems can coordinate translation, review, quality assurance, and content preparation tasks while incorporating human checkpoints for approval and oversight.

We will also walk through the architectural patterns that enable these workflows to run inside customer-controlled and air-gapped environments without transferring sensitive content outside the customer boundary. The session includes a live product demonstration.

Key Takeaways

* Architectural patterns for deploying agentic AI in air-gapped and customer-controlled environments
* How agentic systems can automate localization workflows while preserving critical human review and approval processes
* Practical considerations for operating agentic workflows in regulated environments with auditability and governance requirements

*About the Speaker*

[Shruti Joshi](https://www.linkedin.com/in/28shruti) is building an AI powered secure localization stack for regulated industries such as healthcare, legal, finance that cannot send their content to a typical hosted SaaS. She brings 12+ years of engineering and architecture experience to the question this talk addresses: how do you make an agentic AI system deployable inside a regulated perimeter.

**MCP Is the Interface; Skills Are the Operating Discipline**

This talk shows how MCP and Agent Skills work together in practical agent systems. MCP gives agents a standard interface to tools, data, and workflows; skills encode the operating discipline that makes those connections reliable. Using a sanitized field-operations ledger as the case study, the talk walks through source intake, normalized state, uncertainty labels, role prompts, QA gates, and share-safe status drafting.

*About the Speaker*

[Chuck Hernandez](https://www.linkedin.com/in/chuck-hernandez/) is an AI engineering and client-delivery leader with 10+ years across software, data platforms, and enterprise implementation, including 3+ years shipping production GenAI systems.

**Agentic engineering is about good guidance.**

Garbage Inn. Is garbage out? This is true. For many input and output processes. In biological life and in computer systems, and equally true when working with LLM’s. The better the prompt, the better the context, the better the focus, And the better the contextual awareness, the better the quality of the output the LLM’s generates.
This is the governance, art and practice of what we like to call agentic engineering, something I've been practicing over the last year.

*About the Speaker*

[Dimitri Geelen](https://www.linkedin.com/in/dimitrigeelen/) builds things that don't need him once they're done. Frameworks, transitions, agentic systems — the measure of success is always the same: does it hold up when he leaves the room? He understands not just how to deploy, but what it takes for a new service to survive and scale inside a complex enterprise.

title: Peek Inside an AI Assistant: How It Thinks and Works
location: North York Central Library, 2nd Floor eLearning Lab
description:
You've asked an AI chatbot questions. But there's another kind of AI that doesn't just answer: it acts.
In this demo-driven talk, we'll look deeply at always-on personal AI assistants. The assistant can read your files, use your apps, and remember what you've told it, growing more useful over time. The same powers that let it help you can hurt you if something goes wrong. We'll also open up what happens inside: the hidden instructions, the tools it uses, what it remembers and forgets.
Then we'll look at the AI assistant that helped develop this workshop, and how we shaped our workflow together, and why.
Registration is required and will start September 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM.
Note: Your spot will not be guaranteed after 5 minutes of the start of the program.

title: Paper Trail: Writing and Walking by Sarah Ellis
location: Lillian H. Smith, Lower Level-Auditorium
description:
Photo credit: Thelonius Mthombeni
Join award-winning author, teacher and librarian Sarah Ellis for the upcoming 38th Annual Helen E. Stubbs Memorial Lecture at our Osborne Collection of Early Children’s Books.
The word that best describes Sarah's career in writing is "meander." In this presentation she will tell stories about her work and her wanders, including the pleasures of flaneuring, both on the page and on her feet, the winding journey from grade four essay to substack via a long detour in children's fiction, her beloved companions of the road, the importance of good socks and good colleagues, the inevitable, scary and productive experience of getting lost, and the odd tendency of humans to walk counterclockwise when left to wander freely (true fact!). Come prepared for detours.
Sarah Ellis is the award-winning author of over twenty-five books for children and young adults. In 2013 she was awarded the B.C. Lieutenant Governor’s Award for Literary Excellence. She is a three-time Canadian nominee for the prestigious Astrid Lindgren Memorial Award. Having retired as a children’s librarian and then retired from college teaching she is now writing and reading fulltime in the rain in Vancouver, sharing her bookish thoughts online at "Wild Reading" on substack. Her latest book for children is As Glenn as Can Be illustrated by Nancy Vo, published by Groundwood Books and she has a recent adult memoir, My Year in Fairyland: Grief, MAID and a Lifetime of Reading published by Stonehewer Books.

title: After the Island: Caribbean Canadian Ceramics
location: Gardiner Museum, 111 Queen's Park, Toronto, ON, M5S 2C7, Canada
description:
After the Island: Caribbean Canadian Ceramics                                                                           
        
    




	

	

	


			
Events
	









	

    
        
             
                
                    

October 9, 2026 – April 25, 2027
Exhibition Hall. Third Floor
Included with admission. Free for Gardiner Members



                
                    
    



    
         
    




	


  Get Tickets



  Become a Member






    
         
    






    
        
             
                
                    The Gardiner Museum, Black Artists’ Networks in Dialogue (BAND), and the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) present a landmark curatorial partnership exploring contemporary ceramic practices rooted in Caribbean histories, memory, and cultural transformation. 
Presented across two exhibitions and two cities—Toronto and San Francisco—this collaboration brings together artists whose work examines migration, ornament, labour, ancestry, and the enduring impact of Caribbean cultural traditions across generations and geographies. 
At the Gardiner Museum, After the Island: Caribbean Canadian Ceramics considers how artists of the Caribbean diaspora are embracing the medium of ceramics to explore themes of knowledge transfer and the liberatory potential of the clandestine. Through existing and new work by Caribbean Canadian artists PJ Anderson, Eddy Firmin, Manuel Mathieu, and Sharon Norwood, the exhibition approaches questions of identity, belonging, memory, and cultural continuity through the language of clay. 
At MoAD, After the Island: Ornament and Ceramic Practice in the Jamaican Diaspora focuses on artists whose practices engage Jamaica as memory, inheritance, orientation, and cultural touchstone. The exhibition examines how ornament functions as a carrier of history, labour, ancestral knowledge, and relation across time and distance. 
Together, After the Island: Caribbean Canadian Ceramics and After the Island: Ornament and Ceramic Practice in the Jamaican Diaspora offer a timely exploration of migration, memory, and cultural continuity, demonstrating how artists working with clay continue to create new forms of relation between past and present, homeland and diaspora, history and imagination. 
Throughout both presentations, vessels, decorative forms, sculptural installations, and ceramic surfaces become sites where histories are preserved, challenged, reimagined, and carried forward.

title: Ghost Stories of Toronto: Victorian Spirits
description:
The Victorian age is famously associated with ghost stories, and Victorian Toronto is certainly no exception. For the second talk in this series, author Adam Bunch will explore some of our city's spookiest supernatural tales from the late 1800s, an era that provides us with stories of haunted mansions, secret societies, and the spirits said to roam the halls of some of our finest public buildings.
About this event's guest:
Adam Bunch
Read More:
The Toronto Book of Love
The Toronto Book of the Dead
About this series:
You can learn a lot about Toronto through its ghost stories. Whether you believe in the supernatural or not, the tales we tell about spirits and spectres illuminate the true history of the city. They're often tied to dramatic stories of death and disaster, to fascinating historic sites, and to pivotal moments that helped shape our communities. In this series of talks by author Adam Bunch, we'll explore Toronto's past through tales of ghosts, séances and hauntings. Whether it's phantom horses from the War of 1812, the strange prime minister who believed in the occult, or the ghost who was arrested by the Toronto Police Morality Squad, these supernatural stories have a lot to teach us about the history of the place we call home.

title: Reaping What She Sows: Women at the Forefront of Toronto Food Systems Change
location: Lillian H. Smith
description:
Global events - from pandemics, war, and foodborne illnesses - have threatened farmers' livelihoods, created supermarket shortages, and revealed to consumers that our food system is broken. In the face of these threats to our well-being and food security, what can we do as a community to strengthen our local food system?
Meet
Nancy Matsumoto
, author of
Reaping What She Sows
: How Women Are Rebuilding Our Broken Food System
, who will introduce her book and highlight Toronto women changemakers building up local and regional supply chains to combat the destructive effects of Big Food.
Paul DeCampo
, representative of Karma Co-op Grocery Store will moderate the discussion, which will include the following guest panelists:
Jenn Pfenning
from Pfennings Organic Farm
Sabrina Banh
from Fisherfolk
Together, they will discuss the importance of a resilient, transparent, climate-friendly local and regional food system—for our health, the health of workers, animals and communities, and the future of our planet. Attendees will be inspired to learn how they can also help create positive food system change and contribute to our regional food security.
Presented in celebration of Women's History Month, as part of Small Business Month, and as part of TPL's environmental program series,
Our Fragile Planet
, supported by Friends of Toronto Public Library, South Chapter.
Free program. Please register. The presentation will include an audience Q&A.
Place a hold or borrow from Toronto Public Library:
Reaping What She Sows
: How Women Are Rebuilding Our Broken Food System
(book)
Reaping What She Sows
Reaping What She Sows
Reaping What She Sows
(ebook)
Bio
Nancy Matsumoto
, an award-winning freelance writer and editor who writes about agroecology, food sovereignty, food, drink, and Japanese American culture and history.
Paul DeCampo
has worked as an educator, food researcher and wine marketer. A Karma Co-op Grocery Store member since 1997, Paul has served in various volunteer roles at this community-owned, co-operative grocery store, including on the Board of Directors and as General Manager.

予約規約（⚠️重要）

・当日の不参加、もしくは15分以上の遅刻、また予約取消締切後の変更は原則不参加(No-Show)とみなします。不参加(No-show)が3回になりますと会員登録が抹消され、退会となりますのでご注意ください。

※ご注意※

・空席ができた際は、自動的に”キャンセル待ち”より”参加予定”へ変更されます。この時にMeetupよりお知らせがあるかはわかりません。

title: Poems of Consumption by H. Sinno
location: Aga Khan Museum, 77 Wynford Drive, Toronto, ON M3C 1K1
description:
H.Sinno’s acclaimed performance, Poems of Consumption , reimagines consumer culture through music, poetry, and immersive visuals.

Part concert, part multimedia performance, and part poetic meditation, Poems of Consumption explores the emotional contradictions of modern life through songs built from an unexpected source: Amazon customer reviews transformed into poetry. Partially inspired by Mark Fisher’s Capitalist Realism , Poems of Consumption is a song cycle covering themes like ennui, surveillance capitalism, heartbreak, boycotts, and orientalism, with compositions that juxtapose harsh electronica with the whimsy of a string quartet.

Originally commissioned by London’s Barbican Centre and Shubbak Festival, the production has been praised for its fearless artistic vision and emotional honesty, bringing together experimental music, theatre, and literature into a deeply personal live experience.

title: Python Essentials 1 and 2 Learning Circle
location: York Woods
description:
Learn Python and build your programming skills in a supportive group. This learning circle will meet on Tuesday afternoons from September 22 to December 8, 2-3:30pm. Learning circles are study groups guided by staff for people who want to take a free online course together in a welcoming space. Learners meet weekly and work together through the course materials. Participants are expected to commit to the duration of the course and attend all learning circle sessions.
Learners who successfully complete both courses will earn a digital badge and certificate of completion.
Python Essentials 1
is the first in a 2-course series that teaches computer programming skills including how to design, develop, and improve computer programs using the Python programming language. The course covers essential programming topics such as data types, variables, control flow, functions, and exceptions.
Python Essentials 2
is the second in a 2-course series that will prepare you for the PCAP – Certified Associate in Python Programming certification exam at Pearson VUE. This intermediate-level course covers advanced aspects of Python programming, including modules, packages, exceptions, file processing and object-oriented programming (OOP).
For more information about the Python learning circle, please contact
networkingacademy@tpl.ca

title: Saying Hello to Connecting ft. Nicholas Epley and Gillian Sandstrom
location: Toronto Reference Library, Bram and Bluma Appel Salon, Toronto Reference Library (789 Yonge Street), 2nd floor
description:
This evening will explore the “the liking gap” – how strangers would like us more than we think if we tried to connect.
Make the most of your
Connect IRL
experience by coming before or staying after the featured event. Grab a drink or snack at the bar. This evening's workshop will be announced shortly so stay tuned for that. Try out one of the engagement activities available, including this event's
Conversation Station: The
Bus Stop Challenge
, where you can take a moment or two to connect with a stranger in the most ordinary of small-talk settings.
*****
Join us
in the Toronto Reference Library's Appel Salon
for
Saying Hello to
Reconnecting
,
with psychologists and authors Nicholas Epley and Gillian Sandstrom
in conversation with
Paul Bloom
.
Q&A and book signing to follow. Books available for purchase.
Why do we walk past dozens of strangers a day, headphones in, eyes down, when a two-minute conversation could brighten both of our afternoons? At this event we'll find out what's actually stopping us and then test it. You'll learn what the research says about how strangers respond to being approached, why our predictions are so consistently wrong, and how to start the kind of small, low-stakes conversation that adds up to a bigger life. Then you'll get a chance to have one.
Why do so many of us underestimate the power of a simple "hello"? What is the "liking gap," and how does it keep us from connecting with people who would genuinely enjoy meeting us? And in an age of texting, remote work and screen-mediated relationships, what do we lose when we avoid the small, unscripted moments that once wove strangers into our daily lives?
Nicholas Epley, a University of Chicago psychologist, has spent his career studying this gap. In A Little More Social: How Small Choices Create Unexpected Happiness, Health, and Connection, he argues that connection is a choice we make based on expectations of how others will respond — expectations that skew far too pessimistic. Gillian Sandstrom, Professor in the Psychology of Kindness at the University of Sussex, takes it further in Once Upon a Stranger: The Science of How "Small" Talk Can Add Up to a Big Life, tracing her own path from self-described introvert to leading researcher on talking to strangers.
Come ready to say hello.
About this event’s guests:
Dr. Gillian Sandstrom
Dr. Nicholas Epley
Dr. Paul Bloom
Read More:
Once Upon A Stranger
A Little More Social
The Sweet Spot
***
Connection Workshop (to be announced soon) |
5:30 - 6:30 pm (TBC)
The
Bus Stop Challenge
| 5:30 – 6:30 pm & 8:00 – 9:00 pm
Set up like a familiar TTC platform or bus shelter, this station drops you into the most ordinary of small-talk settings. Draw a prompt card with a simple mission (ask a stranger's opinion, compliment something, trade a recommendation) and see how fast a short, unscripted exchange can turn a stranger into a familiar face. It's the “liking gap”, live and in action.
Connect IRL
is not your average series of events, workshops and activities, but a real chance to connect with other Torontonians in meaningful and sometimes unexpected ways. Through conversation stations meant to spark one-on-one conversations, or hands-on engagement activities and workshops before the featured event, participants can explore the value of connection and community.

title: Engineering leadership: Navigating a changing world
location: Online
description:
Engineering has always addressed challenges by advancing technology. But success now depends not only on technical expertise but also on the ability to connect people, foster collaboration and drive innovation across complex environments.  
What does it take to lead as an engineer in an era defined by AI, global collaboration and rapid change?
Join Professor Emily Moore for an engaging discussion on how engineering careers are evolving and how leaders can adapt to meet new challenges. Drawing on her research into engineering career paths, teamwork and organizational dynamics, Professor Moore will share practical insights on developing the skills that matter for long-term success. Discover how engineers can strengthen their leadership capabilities, navigate change with confidence and amplify their impact in a world where the human side of engineering has never been more important.  
Join us on October 14, 2026 at our monthly Skule™ Lunch & Learn.  
By registering for the Skule™ Lunch & Learn event, you could potentially earn Continuing Professional Development (CPD) credits. CPDs are essential for professional engineers and limited license holders to renew their licenses annually through the PEO PEAK Program. If you’re wondering whether this event offering qualifies you for CPD credits, click here to learn more. 
About the speaker
Professor Emily Moore was appointed Director of Troost Institute for Leadership Education in Engineering (ILead) in October 2018, after more than twenty years in industry. Emily started her career at the Xerox Research Centre of Canada scaling up new materials and processes from the lab to manufacturing. In her 11 years at Xerox, Emily learned a great deal about leading teams and developing new products, becoming a manager and Principal Engineer. Emily then spent 10 years at Hatch, a global engineering firm serving the mining, energy and infrastructure sectors. Emily led international teams to develop new product and service offerings and to deliver major projects, first as the Director of Technology Development and then as Managing Director, Water. Emily was also the inaugural chair of Hatch’s Global Diversity and Inclusion efforts. Emily holds a bachelor’s degree in engineering chemistry from Queen’s University and completed a doctorate in physical chemistry from Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar. In 2016 Emily was recognized as one of 100 Global Inspirational Women in Mining and received the SCI Canada Kalev Pugi Award.

title: How Canadians are Feeling about Democracy These Days
location: North York Central Library, Concourse Event Space
description:
Trust in democratic institutions is being tested in Canada and around the world. Canadians continue to express support for democratic values, yet many are reporting growing concerns about political polarization, declining trust in governments and institutions, misinformation, and whether political systems are responsive to citizens' needs.
Drawing on the latest public opinion research, electoral studies, and engagement data, this panel will examine how Canadians are feeling about democracy today. Are concerns about democratic health widespread or concentrated among particular groups? What is driving shifts in political trust and participation? And what can governments, civil society organizations, educators, and communities do to strengthen democratic resilience and engagement for the future?
Check out the
KnowYourVote.TO
website and the
Celebrate Democracy
page to learn more about Toronto’s upcoming municipal election, access important voter resources, and discover activities and interactive library programs for all ages happening at a branch near you.
This event is generously supported by the McConnell Foundation.

Summary: The adventures of an unusual dog, part St. Bernard, part Scotch shepherd, who is forcibly taken to the Klondike gold fields where he eventually becomes the leader of a wolf pack. Buck is a dog born to luxury, but his life changes dramatically when he is sold to be a sled dog in the Yukon Terrority. He earns a reputation for his strength and courage, and is rescued from a series of bad owners by John Thornton, who teaches him to love. title: We Need To Talk About AI: How Do We Shape AI?
location: Lillian H. Smith, Room B/C
description:
Curious about Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
Join us to learn about and discuss aspects of this technological innovation.
This workshop series explores AI's real impacts on jobs, privacy, the environment, and our communities, while discussing how we can shape it responsibly. Each themed 90-minute session allows for small group discussion, practical takeaways and honest conversation about AI without the hype.
Oct 7 - AI for the Non-Technical
In this session, we tackle the
"Elephant in the Room"
—addressing ethics, hallucinations, and the fear of replacement to foster a responsible
"AI for Good"
mindset. We demystify the technology by viewing AI as an
"intern with a PhD in everything"
—a tool that masters five specific superpowers, such as personalization at scale and rapid research, while leaving the irreplaceable domain of empathy, intuition, and creativity to you.
Oct 14 - How Do We Shape AI?
AI is already reshaping how we work, protect our privacy, and participate in society—yet most of us never get a seat at the table in deciding how it's built or used. This session creates that space. Equal parts presentation and conversation,

title: En Plein Air Connections: Botanical Watercolour in Bloom
location: Toronto Botanical Garden, 777 Lawrence Avenue East, Toronto, ON, M3C 1P2, Canada
description:
Experience the Toronto Botanical Garden through the art of watercolour in this guided outdoor workshop!
Using freshly gathered blooms and botanical patterns as inspiration, you’ll explore approachable painting techniques while incorporating moments of mindfulness that encourage a deeper connection with the natural world. Suitable for all experience levels, this relaxed workshop offers personalized instruction in a welcoming and supportive environment.
 
All materials are provided.
 
Please note: This is an outdoor class that requries about a 10-minute walk with some steep slopes to get to the location. In the case of poor weather, the class will be moved indoors. Please arrive promptly for 1 p.m. We will gather in the Lobby before heading to the outdoor workshop spot.
 
Thursday, October 15, 1 to 3:30 p.m.
Public $80, TBG Members $75 (plus applicable taxes and fees).
 
About Aggie Armstrong
Aggie Armstrong is a Filipino-Canadian artist living and working in Ontario. Working primarily in painting while incorporating hand embroidery and textile elements, she creates layered work inspired by everyday experiences, personal history, and the ways we make sense of the world around us.
 
Her work has been exhibited across Canada, the United States, and France, and she has exhibited at The Artist Project in Toronto since 2022. In 2023, she was commissioned to create the official poster for the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair, and in 2022 she was an artist-in-residence at Château Orquevaux in France. Her work has also been featured in British Vogue, Art Seen Magazine, CTV News, CP24 Breakfast, the Create!, and Colour Me Happy podcasts.
 
Alongside her studio practice, Aggie teaches watercolour workshops throughout the GTA and Southwestern Ontario, creating welcoming, approachable experiences that help people build confidence and discover the joy of painting and creativity.
 
Join Toronto Botanical Garden
 
Join the Toronto Botanical Garden (TBG) as a member to get a discount on this program, upcoming events and classes, and free parking. A TBG membership helps you deepen your knowledge and connection to the natural world, become a part of a dynamic community of plant people, and be inspired! Become a member!

title: Financial Workshops for Seniors
location: Queen/Saulter
description:
Presented by John Stapleton from Open Policy Ontario, learn more about government programs, benefits and eligibility criteria for seniors. These sessions are designed for seniors with low income and those who advise them.
Thursday Oct 1: What Do Seniors Get?
Learn about benefits for older adults living in Ontario, including Canada Pension Plan (CPP), Old Age Security (OAS), Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), and Guaranteed Annual Income Supplement (GAINS).
Thursday Oct 15: Understanding the Personal Income Tax System.
What is a taxable income and how can tax credits, deductions, entitlements and exemptions help to reduce taxable income.
Thursday Oct 29: Protecting Your Retirement Income.
Learn how to reduce claw backs to GIS and GAINS payments if receiving additional income from employment, a private pension, or a Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP).
Thursday Nov 12: Coming to Canada and Leaving Canada.
Learn about eligible benefits for those that resided in Canada for fewer than 40 years between the ages of 18 and 65, or for those planning on emigrating from Canada after retiring.
Thursday Nov 26: Tax Credits and Benefits for Seniors and People with Disabilities.
Learn about other tax credits and benefits for seniors, people with disabilities, and caregivers, including the disability tax credit, the Canada caregiver credit, and the home accessibility tax credit.
Registration not required. Drop-in welcome.

title: History of Philosophy Research Group Talk (Bridger Ehli, IU-Bloomington)
location: Jackman Humanities Building, Room 418, 170 St. George Street, Toronto, Ontario, M5R 2M8, Canada
description:
The History of Modern Philosophy Group is pleased to welcome as its guest speaker Bridger Ehli, an assistant professor in the Department of Philosophy at the University of Indiana – Bloomington. His research concerns themes in epistemology, metaphysics, and the philosophy of mind in early modern European philosophy. He is especially interested in early modern discussions of skepticism, especially as they relate to questions about mental representation, concepts, and the psychology of belief. Most of his work has focused on Hume’s contributions to these issues. In a forthcoming book, he argues that much of Hume’s skepticism arises from his thinking about the limits of intelligibility rather than those of justified belief. 
Details to follow.

Organizations all over the world recognize the value of analytics. Together, we'll learn about the essential tools used in this field.

title: How Do AIs "Think"? And Why They Get Things Wrong
location: North York Central Library, 2nd Floor eLearning Lab
description:
How does a machine actually "think"? Explore the history and latest developments of machine learning.
In this class, we'll dig into what's really going on inside AI systems: how they decide what matters in your question, where their training data comes from (and who's missing from it), and how hidden instructions can sneak into content and hijack an AI. Develop an intuitive understanding of how AIs "think" without the math. We'll talk about how AIs remember, how they don't and how they are both similar and different to humans. And we'll ask the question underneath it all: is there anyone home inside the machine?
Registration is required and will start September 9, 2026 at 9:00 AM.
Note: Your spot will not be guaranteed after 5 minutes of the start of the program.

title: Marina Nemat: Mistress of the Persian Boarding House
location: North York Central Library, Concourse Event Space, North York Central Library (5120 Yonge St), Lower Level
description:
TPL presents internationally bestselling author Marina Nemat in conversation with Farah Heron at the North York Central Library's Concourse Event Space.
In her debut work of historical fiction, Mistress of the Persian Boarding House, Nemat turns to the extraordinary life of her paternal grandmother, Zina, a Russian woman who fled the chaos of the 1917 Revolution and rebuilt her life in Iran. There, in a boarding house that becomes a refuge for other displaced women, Zina forms an unbreakable bond with fellow outsiders from Russia and Iran, women who support one another through childbirth, illness, poverty, political upheaval, and a pandemic. Amid this turmoil, Zina's path crosses with the ambitious Reza Khan, the future Shah of Iran, whose presence in her life becomes both an escape and a source of enduring hardship and sorrow.
Spanning decades and alternating between Zina's years in Russia and her later life in Iran, this sweeping novel asks: what does it mean to build a home and a family from nothing, in the wreckage of empire and revolution?
Drawing on her own family history and her lifelong engagement with themes of exile, resilience, and the search for home, first explored in her internationally bestselling memoir Prisoner of Tehran, Nemat brings the same unflinching honesty and tenderness to her grandmother's story that made her own so unforgettable.
Join Marina Nemat for an intimate conversation about inheritance, chosen family, and the quiet heroism of women who have had to build their lives twice.
Q&A and book signing to follow. Books available for purchase.
About this event’s guests:
Marina Nemat
Farah Heron
Read more:

title: The Grim History of the Death Penalty in Canada
location: Brentwood, Community Room, Ground Floor
description:

Become a page-turner by joining the Between the Lines Book Club! Here, we embark on a new chapter with every read, diving into a world of endless possibilities. Friday September 18
: The Covenant of Water by Abraham Verghese
The Covenant of Water
by Abraham Verghese is a sweeping, richly detailed novel set in Kerala, India, that follows a family across generations as they live with a mysterious condition in which some family members have a fear of water. Beginning in the early 1900s, the story unfolds through the lives of several generations, connecting their personal struggles, relationships, and secrets in unexpected ways. Blending family history, love, loss, medicine, faith, and cultural traditions, the novel explores how the past shapes generations to come. Verghese brings the landscape and people of Kerala vividly to life, while weaving together themes of resilience, sacrifice, healing, and the complicated bonds of family. It is an immersive and emotional story that invites readers to become deeply invested in the lives of its characters and the mysteries that connect them.

title: Ishq Ke Saat Muqaam
location: Aga Khan Museum, 77 Wynford Drive, Toronto, ON M3C 1K1
description:
Ishq Ke Saat Muqaam (The Seven Stages of Love) returns with a renewed artistic vision, bringing together poetry, music, dance, and storytelling to explore one of humanity’s oldest and most profound questions: what does it mean to love?

Written and directed by Nishar Mansuri, the production is inspired by the Sufi understanding of ishq as a path of transformation. Through seven interconnected stages, the work moves from human longing to self-discovery, devotion, and surrender, inviting audiences into a journey that is both deeply personal and universal.

Featuring the poetry of Rumi, Amir Khusrau, Kabir, Bulleh Shah, Hafez, Fariduddin Attar, Sultan Bahu, and other mystic voices, the production reimagines centuries of mystical thought through contemporary performance. Their words become the foundation for an experience that transcends borders, languages, and faith traditions, inviting audiences to reflect on love as a force that connects us all.

location: Aga Khan Museum, 77 Wynford Drive, Toronto, ON M3C 1K1
description:
Discover the beauty and meaning behind Fasayfisa’ — an Arabic term for small, colourful pieces of marble or stone arranged side by side to form a unified design.

Through this hands-on workshop, participants will create a small ornament using vibrant glass tiles, inspired by the intricate patterns found in Islamic art and architecture. Drawing from examples in the Aga Khan Museum Collections, explore how these repeating designs embody harmony, balance, and creativity, a tradition that has flourished for centuries.

title: Birding with Beni: Fall Birding
location: Toronto Botanical Garden, 777 Lawrence Avenue East, Toronto, ON, M3C 1P2, Canada
description:
Join us for a fall birding nature walk!
Fall migration is well underway! Join TBG Horticulturist and avid birder Sasan Beni for an engaging walk through the gardens and Wilket Creek Ravine, as you seek out the wildlife that call this place home. Learn how to identify the many different species passing through and how you can help them in their journey.
 
Bring your binoculars for a better view (we will have extras on hand) and a mug/thermos for a warm beverage and post-birding chat.
 
As with any wildlife tour, the spotting of birds and other wildlife is not guaranteed and is not within the control of the tour guide. Please be patient and considerate. The tour will not be rescheduled due to a lack of bird sightings. The tour will only be rescheduled due to inclement weather.
 
Meet at the TBG main entrance, just outside the George and Kathy Dembroski Centre for Horticulture.
 
Saturday, October 17, 8 to 10 a.m.
Public $22, Members $20 (plus applicable taxes and fees).
 
About Sasan Beni
Sasan Beni is a writer turned horticulturist. He graduated with a diploma in Environmental Landscape Management from Seneca College in King City, worked for the Toronto Zoo as a seasonal gardener, and joined TBG in 2020 as a seasonal Horticulturalist. His home is a revolving door of tropical plants. Beni is also passionate about birdwatching and wildlife photography. In the last three years, he has led many guided birdwatching walks around Toronto and has written several articles for Trellis magazine illustrated with his nature photographs.
 
Join Toronto Botanical Garden
Join the Toronto Botanical Garden (TBG) as a member to get a discount on this program, upcoming events and classes, and free parking. A TBG membership helps you deepen your knowledge and connection to the natural world, become a part of a dynamic community of plant people, and be inspired! Become a member!
 
Accessibility
The walk will be at a leisurely pace throughout, following designated pathways and trails but sometimes covering uneven terrain and steep inclines. Dress appropriately for the weather and walk slowly. Wearing layers is recommended. Closed-toed shoes are required. We will begin promptly. 
NOTE: This program occurs rain or shine (save for cases of extreme weather); please dress appropriately for the weather.
 
Additional Program Information



Please review our Refund Policy and Terms of Agreement.
For more information on accessibility at the garden please review our Accessibility Features webpage. If you have any accessibility requirements during your program please email programsupport@torontobotanicalgarden.ca.
To learn more about the Toronto Botanical Garden and our programs, please review our list of Frequently Asked Questions.

Meet the Resident:
Sarah Zanchetta (she/they) is a queer textile artist and educator whose practice dives into the loss of connection and knowledge of poisonous plants in North America. title: Mold-Making 101 with Janet Macpherson | 2 Weekends
location: 300 Campbell Avenue, Unit 115, Toronto, ON
description: Dates : Saturday and Sunday October 17-18 & 24-25 2026 Times : 10:00am - 4:00pm Location : 300 Campbell Avenue, Unit 115 Instructor : Janet Macpherson Unlock new creative possibilities in ceramics with our comprehensive Mold-Making 101 course. This hands-on class will guide you through the process of designing and creating plaster molds for both slip casting and press molding techniques. You’ll learn how to craft one-part and two-part molds, make decorative sprig molds, and combine slip-cast pieces into finished ceramic forms. This course is best for those with some hand-building experience. Throughout the course, you'll explore: - The fundamentals of plaster and its use in mold-making. - Techniques for creating and using press molds and sprig molds. - How to design and construct two-part molds for more complex shapes. - The basics of slip casting and assembling multi-part pieces. - Finishing techniques to prepare your work for firing and glazing. What you'll take home: - Your Molds of course! - 1 - 3 Slip cast pieces of each mold you complete Please note: 1) Glazing is not part of this course. You can book a glazing session seperately ($50) by emailing the technician at our Dupont Location. Glazing sessions include the use of our studio glazes. Firing fee is included. 2) Due to the hands-on and cumulative nature of this course, it's important to attend each session as we may not be able to repeat material covered in a missed class in a thorough way although we will try to catch you up. 3) By the end of the course, you'll have developed a new set of skills, a collection of unique molds, and the confidence to continue exploring mold-making in your own creative practice. ALL WORKSHOPS ARE NON REFUNDABLE

title: Wildlife-friendly Fall Gardens
location: Toronto Reference Library, Room B1 (located in the basement)
description:
At this time of year, many people admire the fall colours but also feel the need to rake and dispose of leaves, cut dead stems, and remove fallen branches. But what if this tidying up negatively affects our gardens and pollinators? While we may not see the bees and butterflies during the fall and winter, they are still around!
In this presentation, Dorte Windmuller, a Butterflyway Ranger of the David Suzuki Foundation, will discuss how to maintain and protect wildlife habitat even throughout the colder months, and how “leave the leaves” can help nature come back stronger the next season.

title: Ishq Ke Saat Muqaam
location: Aga Khan Museum, 77 Wynford Drive, Toronto, ON M3C 1K1
description:
Ishq Ke Saat Muqaam (The Seven Stages of Love) returns with a renewed artistic vision, bringing together poetry, music, dance, and storytelling to explore one of humanity’s oldest and most profound questions: what does it mean to love?

Written and directed by Nishar Mansuri, the production is inspired by the Sufi understanding of ishq as a path of transformation. Through seven interconnected stages, the work moves from human longing to self-discovery, devotion, and surrender, inviting audiences into a journey that is both deeply personal and universal.

Featuring the poetry of Rumi, Amir Khusrau, Kabir, Bulleh Shah, Hafez, Fariduddin Attar, Sultan Bahu, and other mystic voices, the production reimagines centuries of mystical thought through contemporary performance. Their words become the foundation for an experience that transcends borders, languages, and faith traditions, inviting audiences to reflect on love as a force that connects us all.

title: Paper Quilling: Fall Tree Workshop
location: Toronto Botanical Garden, 777 Lawrence Avenue East, Toronto, ON, M3C 1P2, Canada
description:
Celebrate the magic of autumn with a relaxing day of creativity at the beautiful Toronto Botanical Garden!
Join artist Deepa Krishnan for a fun, beginner-friendly paper quilling workshop. In this 4-hour session, you’ll learn a variety of quilling techniques while creating a stunning fall tree on an 8”x10” canvas. Inspired by the rich colours of the season, you’ll have the freedom to choose your own autumn palette, making your artwork truly one of a kind.
 
This workshop includes a 30-minute lunch break. We recommend bringing your own lunch to enjoy while taking in the beautiful surroundings of the garden.
 
Whether you’re trying paper quilling for the first time or looking to expand your skills, this workshop is a wonderful way to slow down, get creative, and celebrate the beauty of the season.
 
All supplies are included, and no prior experience needed. This workshop is suitable for adults and children ages 12 and above.
 
Sunday, October 18, 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m.
Public $100, TBG Members $90 (plus applicable taxes and fees).
 
About Deepa Krishnan
Deepa Krishnan is a self-taught artist specializing in the art of paper quilling, which involves manipulating narrow strips of paper to create exquisite designs. She discovered this art form when she was looking for a creative outlet from her engineering job. She was amazed by the possibilities and beauty of paper quilling, that she decided to pursue it as a full-time career. Since then, she has been passionately mastering this technique and has created many artworks drawing inspiration from nature, music and travel. She cuts the paper strips in different widths to add depth and dimension to her creations. She loves to play with the colours and experiment with the quilling techniques to create her own distinctive style. Deepa believes that anyone can learn this art form, regardless of their age or skill level, and she hosts many workshops to spread the joy of quilling. She enjoys seeing her students discover their own creativity and style in paper quilling.
 
Join Toronto Botanical Garden
Join the Toronto Botanical Garden (TBG) as a member to get a discount on this program, upcoming events and classes, and free parking. A TBG membership helps you deepen your knowledge and connection to the natural world, become a part of a dynamic community of plant people, and be inspired! Become a member!

For more information on accessibility at the garden please review our Accessibility Features webpage. If you have any accessibility requirements during your program please email programsupport@torontobotanicalgarden.ca.

Empire of Pain
by Patrick Radden Keefe is a gripping nonfiction account of the Sackler family, whose immense wealth and influence were built through Purdue Pharma and the marketing of OxyContin. Blending investigative journalism, family saga, and social history, the book explores the rise of a powerful dynasty and its central role in the opioid crisis. This thought-provoking read raises important questions about corporate responsibility, wealth, power, and accountability.
Participants can borrow a copy of the book from the Woodside Square branch upon registration.
